items.title: Section: Closing Confused Conduct, and Which Afflictions Reference a Real Object

items.zh: 見取、戒禁取及貪瞋等，緣見為境、見所斷者，彼一切皆是執邪了行。即此一切迷苦、集諦者，是迷彼因緣所依處行。即此一切迷滅、道諦者，是迷彼怖畏生行。即彼一切任運所起修道斷者，是任運現行迷執行。復次，如前所說一切煩惱障治差別，但依化宜顯示麁相，建立煩惱迷執邪行。為令所化有情於種種煩惱諸行過失易生解故，今當總辯一切煩惱如實巨細之相，建立迷執諸行差別。問：如是諸煩惱幾有事？幾無事？答：諸見與慢是無事，於諸行中實無有我而分別轉故。貪、恚是有事。無明、疑通二種。
items.en: View-attachment, precept-attachment, and greed, hatred, and the rest that take a view as their object and are severed at the path of seeing, are all wrongly understanding conduct joined with attachment. All of this delusion about the truths of suffering and origination is conduct confused about their causes, conditions, and basis. All of this delusion about the truths of cessation and the path is conduct arising from that fear. All of this affliction arising spontaneously, severed by the path of cultivation, is spontaneously manifesting confused conduct. Question: of these afflictions, how many reference a real object, and how many do not? Answer: views and conceit are without a real object, since they discriminate a self where, among the formations, no self genuinely exists. Greed and hatred reference a real object. Ignorance and doubt run through both.

items.title: Section: Which Afflictions Arise Spontaneously With Every Kind of Feeling

items.zh: 問：是諸煩惱，幾與樂根相應？乃至幾與捨根相應？答：若任運生一切煩惱，皆於三受現行可得。是故通一切識身者，與一切根相應；不通一切識身者，與意地一切根相應。不任運生一切煩惱，隨其所應諸根相應，我今當說。
items.en: Question: of these afflictions, how many correspond to the pleasant faculty, and so on through the neutral faculty? Answer: if affliction arises spontaneously, all such affliction can manifest amid any of the three feelings. Therefore, affliction common to all consciousness-bodies corresponds to every faculty; affliction not common to all consciousness-bodies corresponds only to every faculty within the mental ground. Affliction not arising spontaneously corresponds to its respective faculties accordingly, which shall now be explained.

items.title: Section: Greed and Hatred Through the Five Feelings

items.zh: 貪於一時樂、喜相應，或於一時憂、苦相應，或於一時與捨相應。問：如何等？答：如有一，或於樂受起會遇愛、不乖離愛而現在前，遂於樂受不會遇、非會遇，若乖離、非和合；或於苦受起不會愛、若乖離愛而現在前，遂於苦受合會、非不合會，不乖離、非乖離。由是因緣，貪於一時憂、苦相應。與此相違，喜、樂相應。若於不苦不樂位而生味著，當知此貪捨根相應。恚於一時憂、苦相應，或有一時喜、樂相應。問：如何等？答：如有一，自然為苦逼切身心，遂於內苦作意思惟，發恚恨心；或於非愛諸行有情及諸法所作意思惟，發恚恨心。由是故恚憂、苦相應。問：恚與喜、樂相應，如何等？答：如有一，於怨家等非愛有情起恚惱心，作意思惟：願彼沒苦，沒已不濟；或不得樂，得已還失，若遂所願，便生喜、樂。由是故恚喜、樂相應。
items.en: Greed at times corresponds to pleasure and joy, at times to distress and pain, and at times to neutral feeling. If one generates a wish for union with pleasant feeling and non-separation from it, yet that pleasant feeling is not met, or is met with separation rather than union; or generates a wish for non-union with painful feeling and separation from it, yet that painful feeling is met with union rather than separation — for these reasons, greed at times corresponds to distress and pain. The opposite corresponds to joy and pleasure. If attachment arises with respect to the neutral state, this greed should be known to correspond to the neutral faculty. Hatred at times corresponds to distress and pain, and at times to joy and pleasure. If one is naturally pressed upon in body and mind by suffering, and thereupon reflects inwardly on that suffering, giving rise to a resentful, hateful mind; or reflects upon disagreeable formations, beings, or things, giving rise to a resentful, hateful mind — for these reasons, hatred corresponds to distress and pain. If one generates a hateful, malicious mind towards an enemy or other disagreeable being, reflecting: may they sink into misery, and once sunk, be unaided; or may they fail to attain happiness, or having attained it, lose it again — and this wish is then fulfilled, joy and pleasure arise. For this reason, hatred corresponds to joy and pleasure.

items.title: Section: Self-View, Wrong View, and the Perverse Comfort of Denying Karma

items.zh: 薩迦耶見及邊執見，若於樂俱行蘊觀我我所，或觀為常，喜根相應。若於苦俱行蘊觀我我所，或觀為常，憂根相應。若於捨俱行蘊觀我我所，或觀為常，捨根相應。斷見攝邊執見，當知一切與彼相違。見取、戒禁取，取彼見故，隨其所應，如彼相應。邪見一種，先作妙行，憂根相應；先作惡行，喜根相應。
items.en: Self-view and extreme-view, if they regard the aggregates accompanying pleasant feeling as self or self-belonging, or regard them as permanent, correspond to the joyful faculty. If they regard the aggregates accompanying painful feeling this way, they correspond to the distressed faculty. If they regard the aggregates accompanying neutral feeling this way, they correspond to the neutral faculty. Extreme-view of the annihilationist kind should be known to run entirely opposite to this. View-attachment and precept-attachment, taking that view as their object, correspond accordingly, just as that view does. Wrong view alone: in one who has previously performed virtuous deeds, it corresponds to the distressed faculty; in one who has previously performed unwholesome deeds, it corresponds to the joyful faculty.

items.zh: 慢於一時喜根相應，或於一時憂根相應。問：如何等？

items.title: Section: Relief in Doubting Bad News — Conceit, Doubt, and Ignorance

items.zh: 答：略有二慢。一、高舉慢，二、卑下慢。又高舉慢，有三高舉。何等為三？謂稱量高舉、解了高舉、利養高舉。此高舉慢，喜根相應。若卑下慢，與彼相違，憂根相應。疑，若於利養、恭敬、稱譽、樂善趣等決定事中，他所導引令猶豫者，憂根相應。於無利養、不敬、譏毀、苦惡趣等決定事中，他所導引令猶豫者，喜根相應。無明，通與五根相應。所餘相應，引事指斥，文不復現。先辯煩惱諸根相應，但約麁相道理建立，令初行者解無亂故。今約巨細道理建立，令久行者了自他身種種行解差別轉故。
items.en: Answer: in brief, there are two kinds of conceit. First, elevated conceit. Second, lowly conceit. This elevated conceit corresponds to the joyful faculty. Lowly conceit, opposite to that, corresponds to the distressed faculty. Doubt, if someone is led by another to waver regarding the settled matters of gain, honour, praise, and a pleasant destiny, corresponds to the distressed faculty. If someone is led by another to waver regarding the settled matters of no gain, disrespect, mockery, and a painful destiny, it corresponds to the joyful faculty. Ignorance corresponds indiscriminately to all five faculties. The correspondence of the rest, illustrated by example, does not appear again in the text. The earlier explanation of affliction's correspondence with the faculties was established only according to coarse principles, so that beginning practitioners might understand without confusion. This present explanation is established according to both coarse and fine principles, so that long-practising students might understand the many differing turnings of conduct and understanding in themselves and others.

blocks.text: Which feelings go with which afflictions. The treatise is frank: affliction can feel good.
Views and pride discriminate a self where none exists. Master Cháng Bǎi: greed and hatred arise on conventionally real objects, lovely or unlovely.
Master Cháng Bǎi: afflictions common to all six consciousnesses go with all feelings; those only of the mental ground go with joy, sorrow, and equanimity.

Master Cháng Bǎi: wanting pleasure and not getting it, greed goes with sorrow. And hatred can go with joy: when an enemy's misfortune truly comes about, joy arises. The treatise is frank about the pleasure of an enemy's misfortune.
Master Cháng Bǎi: regarding good deeds done in the past, the one who denies karma feels regret; regarding bad deeds, believing no result will come, they feel joy.
Master Cháng Bǎi: doubt about good prospects saddens; doubt about bad news is a relief. The earlier, simpler account was for new students; this one is for those who have practised long.
"Doubting bad news is a relief." The treatise notices how affliction disguises itself as comfort.

quiz.q: The English has "conduct rooted in that cause and basis." What is left out?
options: it omits 迷: the cause and basis is what is confused about, and "rooted in" makes it the source
nothing: these afflictions grow from suffering and origin, so that "rooted in" is right, 迷 being a mere modifier
it omits 彼, which should be "his"
it omits 行, which should be "walking"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: this is the mental activity of affliction confused about the causal basis of worldly cause and effect, that is, about the truths of suffering and origin. The cause and basis is the object of confusion. The English drops 迷 and reads it as the source of the conduct.

quiz.q: What conduct are those taking views as object, those confused about cessation, and those of cultivation?
options: joined with attachment; arising from fear; spontaneously manifesting
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: view-attachment grasps the three incorrect views; about accomplishing the path and realising cessation the mind is confused and afraid; and spontaneously arising subtle afflictions are innate, not from improper attention. These complete the seven kinds of confused conduct.

quiz.q: How many afflictions have a real object, how many not, and why?
options: greed and hatred lack it, views and conceit having concrete objects and the former being passing moods, ignorance and doubt lacking it wholly
views and conceit lack it; greed and hatred have it; ignorance and doubt run through both
quiz.why: Views and conceit discriminate a self where none exists. Master Cháng Bǎi: greed and hatred arise on the conventionally real lovely or unlovely objects, and so are said to have a real object. The English "reference a real object" is workable, though §15 of fascicle 58 phrased this less well.

quiz.q: How do spontaneous afflictions correspond with faculties, for those common or not to all consciousness-bodies?
options: only with equanimity, being subtle; those of all consciousnesses with equanimity and the rest with pain
they manifest in all three feelings; those of all consciousnesses go with every faculty, those of mind alone with joy, sorrow, equanimity
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: what extends to the five sense-consciousnesses and the sixth is common to all; afflictions only of the mental ground go only with joy, sorrow, and equanimity; non-conceptual or innate ones are called spontaneous. Elsewhere the lecture slips on this; the answer follows the Sub-commentary's agreed reading.

quiz.q: Why can greed correspond with sorrow and pain?
options: one wants pleasure and misses it, or wants no pain and meets it, wishes being thwarted
greed itself is painful, always joined to sorrow, the treatise's joining it to pleasure being only a worldly view the lecture rejects
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: wanting pleasant feeling without getting it, greed goes with sorrow; not wanting pain yet meeting it, it goes with pain; when what appears is the reverse of what is sought, greed goes with sorrow and pain. The English follows this well.

quiz.q: When does greed correspond to equanimity?
options: when relish arises in the neither-pain-nor-pleasure state
when pain is so deep the mind numbs
quiz.why: The treatise says attachment in the neutral state goes with equanimity. Master Cháng Bǎi: if relish and attachment arise towards formations in the neither-painful-nor-pleasant state, this is such greed. So equanimity here is only a feeling tone, not the virtue.

quiz.q: How can hatred correspond with joy and pleasure?
options: wishing an enemy's misery, and that being fulfilled, joy arises
the angry are energetic and feel relief after an outburst, a physical fact unrelated to whether a wish is fulfilled
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: this being makes such a wish in hatred, and when it truly comes about, joy and pleasure arise. The treatise's example is frank about the pleasure of an enemy's misfortune. Note the joy here is a defiled joy joined to hatred, not spiritual joy.

quiz.q: With which faculty do self-view and extreme view go regarding aggregates with pleasant, painful, and neutral feeling?
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: one regards the aggregates accompanying pleasure as self, as belonging to self, or as permanent. Since views belong to the mental ground, the faculties are joy, sorrow, and equanimity, not bodily pleasure and pain. The English "joyful" and "distressed" fit.

quiz.q: How do view-attachment and precept-attachment correspond with faculties?
options: only with joy, grasping one's view always pleasing, differing from self-view, as the lecture stresses, 如彼相應 being only general
they grasp those views, and so correspond just as those views do
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: these two grasp the self-view and extreme view just mentioned, and so their correspondence with the five feeling faculties is the same as theirs. The English "taking that view as their object" is accurate.

quiz.q: The English has "Wrong view, having previously performed virtuous deeds." What is wrong with the subject, and what is the point?
options: the subject is right, the view itself performing deeds
the person acts, not the view; one denying causality regrets past good deeds and delights over bad ones
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: regarding good deeds done in the past, one feels regret, going with sorrow; regarding bad deeds, one believes no bad result will come and goes with joy. The person acted, not the view. The English participle makes wrong view the doer. A vivid passage: denial of karma brings perverse comfort.

quiz.q: The English §13 opens "Answer: in brief, there are two kinds of conceit." What was dropped?
options: nothing: wrong view at §12 is the question here, and the three elations are the lecturer's additions, rightly excluded
it drops the statement on conceit's feelings, the question, and the three elations, so that the answer hangs
quiz.why: The lecture's source has the sentence that conceit goes at times with joy and at times with sorrow, a question, and three elations. Master Cháng Bǎi: elated conceit arising in these three ways makes one glad; lowly conceit goes with sorrow because one's conditions really fall short. The English has lost the setup.

quiz.q: Why can doubt go with sorrow or with joy?
options: wavering about good things saddens; wavering about bad things gladdens
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: these things were good, and one once thought them excellent, but now one is undecided. So doubt about good prospects saddens; doubt about a bad outcome is a relief. The English "led by another to waver" keeps 他所導引 well.

quiz.q: Why does the account of faculties here differ from the earlier one?
options: the earlier was outsiders' and wrong, corrected here, everyone needing to read only this account
earlier was coarse for beginners; this is coarse and fine, for long practitioners
the earlier concerns the desire realm
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the earlier account was set up by coarse principle, so that new students understand without confusion; this one lets long-practising disciples see the differing activity of body, mind, and affliction in self and others. A fine statement of graded teaching.
